Decomposition as features for global models

For machine-learning forecasters (ts6), decomposition outputs become features: the trend strength and seasonal strength of each series, its recent seasonally adjusted level, the seasonal index for the target period. Global models also commonly normalise each series by its recent level so they can share patterns across series of very different sizes; dividing by a seasonally adjusted level, rather than a raw recent mean, avoids confusing "this is December" with "this product grew". Large-scale studies of forecasting competitions have used exactly these features to predict which forecasting method will work best on each series.

Decomposition is not causal

A decomposition says how variation is distributed over time, not why. A rising trend could be population growth, price increases, a successful marketing campaign or the slow loss of a competitor, and the decomposition cannot tell them apart. Business users often read "trend up 3%" as "we are doing better", when inflation was 3%. Pair decompositions with the obvious adjustments (inflation, population, number of stores open) and with domain knowledge before telling a story about them, and leave causal claims to the methods of ts11.
prod:
The Prophet story: forecasting at scale with analysts in the loop

Taylor and Letham's paper starts from an organisational problem, not a statistical one. They observed that fully automatic forecasting tools were often brittle and too inflexible to accept useful assumptions, while analysts able to produce good forecasts by hand were rare, so demand for forecasts far exceeded supply. Their answer had two halves. The model half was the decomposition above, with parameters an analyst could understand without knowing time-series theory: a capacity for saturating growth, known changepoints such as a product launch, a holiday list, and smoothing knobs. The process half was simulated historical forecasts: produce forecasts from many past origins (they discuss horizons such as 30, 90, 180 or 365 days), compare them with simple baselines including a seasonal-naive forecast and an automatically chosen ARIMA, and surface the series where Prophet does badly, in priority order, so an analyst can inspect them. Their worked example is the number of Events created on Facebook, a daily series with a trend change, yearly and weekly seasonality and holiday spikes. The paper's evaluation idea — many origins, compared with baselines, per horizon — is exactly the backtesting discipline of ts5.

Prophet became one of the most widely used forecasting libraries because it made reasonable forecasts easy for non-specialists. Its reputation since has been mixed: on benchmark collections of series, simpler methods often match it, mainly because it ignores short-term autocorrelation. The lesson for an engineer is to treat it like any other method: a candidate in a backtest, judged against seasonal-naive and exponential smoothing, not a default.

Failure modes you will meet

Holiday calendars that are wrong or incomplete. A forecast for India that lacks Diwali, or for the US that lacks a new federal holiday, will place demand in the wrong week. Symptoms: large errors that recur on the same calendar events. Keep holiday tables per country and per region, versioned and tested, and include the days before and after where shopping actually happens.

A distorted year poisoning the seasonal pattern. When a year contains something extraordinary — a pandemic lockdown, a months-long outage, a one-off mega-promotion — a decomposition that treats it as normal bakes it into the seasonal factors for years. Symptoms: forecasts that predict last year's anomaly again. Mark such periods as outliers or level shifts so they sit in the remainder, or exclude them when estimating seasonality.

Additive treatment of multiplicative growth. When a business doubles, an additive seasonal pattern estimated in its smaller years under-forecasts the peak season, in exactly the month where stock-outs are most expensive. Symptoms: residuals that are large and of the same sign every peak season. Check the swing against the level and log if needed.

Daylight saving and time zones in hourly data. The day the clocks change has 23 or 25 hours; an hourly seasonal pattern indexed by local clock hour sees a missing or doubled hour. Store in UTC, derive local-time features explicitly, and decide whether the daily cycle follows the local clock (human activity does) or the sun.

What to monitor

In production, monitor the remainder, not just the forecast error. A healthy decomposition's remainder has no structure: check its autocorrelation at the seasonal lags each time the model is re-fitted, and alert if seasonal strength or trend strength of a series changes sharply between re-fits — that usually means a data problem or a real change in behaviour worth a human look. Keep the decomposition settings (period, transform, windows, holiday table version) in the model's metadata, so that a change in output can be traced to a change in input or configuration.

Knobs

The knobs that matter are the transform (none, log, Box-Cox λ), the period or periods, the seasonal window (how fast the pattern may change), the trend window or changepoint prior (how fast the trend may bend), the number of Fourier pairs per period, the holiday list and window, and the outlier treatment. Each one should be chosen by backtesting forecasts that use it over several origins, and the choice re-checked when the series' behaviour changes.
myths: Decomposition is a forecasting model.

Classical decomposition and STL are descriptive: they explain the past. To forecast you still have to project the trend (with some model) and repeat the seasonal pattern, and the trend estimate is least reliable at the very end of the series, exactly where the forecast starts. Prophet is a forecasting model built on a decomposition, which is different.
Seasonality and cycles are the same thing.

Seasonality repeats with a fixed, known period tied to the calendar or clock: 7 days, 12 months, 24 hours. A cycle rises and falls without a fixed period, like a business cycle that lasts anywhere from two to ten years. You can put a seasonal term in a model; you cannot do that for a cycle, because you do not know when the next turn comes.
If the seasonal swing grows over time, you need a fancy model.

Usually you need a log. When the seasonal swing grows in proportion to the level, the components multiply, and the log turns multiplication into addition: a December that is always 20% above trend becomes a constant +0.18 in log units. Fit additively on the log scale and exponentiate back.
A yearly seasonal pattern handles every holiday.

Only holidays that fall on the same date each year. Easter, Ramadan, Diwali, Chinese New Year and Thanksgiving move around the calendar, so a 'same day last year' pattern smears them across the wrong weeks. They need explicit holiday features, as Prophet's h(t) term provides.
The seasonally adjusted figure is the raw figure with noise removed.

It is the raw figure with the seasonal component removed; the noise is still in it. Seasonally adjusted series are also revised as new data arrives, because the seasonal factors near the end of the series are re-estimated once later data exists.
lab:
Goal: decompose a synthetic monthly series whose seasonal swing grows with its level, see why the log scale is right for it, and fit Prophet-style Fourier seasonality with different numbers of harmonics. NumPy and pandas from gpt_env (Python 3.12). Save as ts2.py.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n, m = 72, 12                                   # six years of monthly data, yearly season
t = np.arange(n)
trend = 1000 * 1.02 ** (t / 1)                  # +2% a month: the level more than quadruples
season = 1 + 0.25 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / m) + 0.10 * np.cos(4 * np.pi * t / m)
y = pd.Series(trend * season * rng.lognormal(0, 0.03, n),
              index=pd.date_range("2019-01-01", periods=n, freq="MS"))

def classical(series, m, kind):
    """Classical decomposition: centred 2xm moving average, then average seasonal deviations."""
    x = np.log(series) if kind == "log" else series
    tr = x.rolling(m, center=True).mean().rolling(2).mean().shift(-1)   # 2xm-MA for even m
    detr = x - tr
    s = detr.groupby(detr.index.month).transform("mean")
    s = s - s.iloc[:m].mean()                   # make the seasonal pattern sum to zero
    resid = x - tr - s
    return tr, s, resid

for kind in ("additive", "log"):
    tr, s, r = classical(y, m, kind)
    early, late = r.iloc[6:30].std(), r.iloc[42:66].std()
    strength = max(0.0, 1 - r.var() / (s + r).var())
    print(f"{kind:8s}: residual sd first half {early:8.3f}, second half {late:8.3f}, "
          f"seasonal strength {strength:.3f}")

# Prophet-style seasonality: regress log(y) on a linear trend plus K Fourier pairs
ly = np.log(y.values)
for K in (1, 2, 3, 6):
    cols = [np.ones(n), t]
    for k in range(1, K + 1):
        cols += [np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * t / m), np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * t / m)]
    X = np.column_stack(cols)
    train, test = slice(0, 60), slice(60, 72)       # fit on 5 years, forecast the 6th
    w, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X[train], ly[train], rcond=None)
    pred = np.exp(X[test] @ w)
    mape = np.mean(np.abs(pred - y.values[test]) / y.values[test]) * 100
    print(f"K={K}: {X.shape[1]:2d} columns, test MAPE {mape:5.2f}%")

# Seasonal-naive for comparison: next year's month = this year's same month
sn = y.values[48:60]
print(f"seasonal naive test MAPE {np.mean(np.abs(sn - y.values[60:]) / y.values[60:]) * 100:5.2f}%")

Run: python ts2.py. Output from a test run:

additive: residual sd first half  149.895, second half  180.994, seasonal strength 0.879
log     : residual sd first half    0.024, second half    0.026, seasonal strength 0.986
K=1:  4 columns, test MAPE  6.17%
K=2:  6 columns, test MAPE  2.99%
K=3:  8 columns, test MAPE  2.85%
K=6: 14 columns, test MAPE  2.97%
seasonal naive test MAPE 20.18%

What to look for. On the raw scale the remainder grows from the first half to the second (the additive model cannot keep up with a widening swing), and seasonal strength is lower because seasonal misfit is dumped into the remainder. On the log scale the remainder is the same size throughout (about 0.025, i.e. 2.5% noise — the generator used 3%) and seasonal strength is near 1. The Fourier fit improves sharply from one harmonic to two, because the true pattern has a second harmonic, and then stops improving: six pairs is the maximum for m = 12 and only adds noise. Seasonal-naive loses badly here because it carries last year's level forward and ignores 27% yearly growth.

Try next. Set the second-harmonic amplitude to 0 and check that K = 1 now suffices. Add an Easter-like spike in a different month each year and watch it leak into the classical seasonal estimates for two months.
recap: A decomposition splits a series into a trend (the slow-moving level), a seasonal component (a pattern that repeats with a fixed period) and a remainder (everything else).
Components add when the seasonal swing stays the same size as the level changes, and multiply when the swing grows with the level; taking logs turns a multiplicative series into an additive one.

Classical decomposition estimates the trend with a centred moving average (a 2×m moving average when the period m is even), averages the detrended values for each season, and centres those averages to sum to zero.
Classical decomposition loses the trend at both ends, assumes the seasonal pattern never changes and is thrown off by outliers.
STL uses local regression (loess) to let the seasonal pattern evolve slowly, gives estimates at the ends, and can down-weight outliers with robustness weights.
Several seasonal periods (daily, weekly, yearly) can be handled with MSTL or with Fourier terms, where a handful of sine and cosine pairs approximate any smooth repeating shape.
Holidays that move around the calendar, trading days and month lengths need explicit adjustment; a fixed seasonal pattern cannot capture them.
Trend and seasonal strength measures compare the remainder's variance with the variance of the component plus remainder; values near 1 mean a strong component.
Prophet models a series as trend plus Fourier seasonality plus holidays plus error, fitted as a regression, with automatically placed changepoints and an analyst in the loop.
glossary: y = trend + seasonal + remainder. Right when the seasonal swing is roughly the same size whatever the level.
A family of power transforms indexed by λ that includes the log (λ = 0); used to make the seasonal swing and the noise roughly constant in size.
The average of a window of values placed symmetrically around each point, used to estimate the trend.
A moment where the trend's growth rate is allowed to change; Prophet places many candidate changepoints and shrinks most of their effects to zero.
The 1920s method that estimates the trend with a centred moving average and the seasonal component by averaging the detrended values for each season.
Rises and falls without a fixed period, such as a business cycle; different from seasonality.
Pairs of sine and cosine waves at the seasonal frequency and its multiples; a weighted sum of a few pairs can approximate any smooth repeating pattern.
A sine or cosine whose frequency is a whole multiple of the base seasonal frequency; the k-th harmonic completes k cycles per season.
Locally weighted regression: fit a simple line around each point using nearby points, with closer points weighted more, and read the smoothed value off it.
A holiday whose calendar date changes from year to year, such as Easter, Ramadan or Diwali.
Multiple STL: applies STL repeatedly to extract several seasonal components, such as daily and weekly cycles in hourly data.
y = trend × seasonal × remainder. Right when the seasonal swing grows in proportion to the level.
The number of observations in one seasonal cycle: 4 for quarterly data with a yearly season, 12 for monthly, 7 for daily data with a weekly cycle.
An open-source forecasting library from Facebook (2017) that fits trend, Fourier seasonality and holiday effects as a regression.
What is left after removing trend and seasonality; also called the residual or irregular component.
Weights STL assigns to each point after a first pass, close to zero for points with huge remainders, so outliers stop distorting the trend and season.
max(0, 1 − Var(remainder) / Var(seasonal + remainder)); near 1 means seasonality dominates the non-trend variation.
A pattern that repeats with a fixed, known period, such as weekly or yearly.
The original series with the seasonal component removed (subtracted, or divided out), used to see the underlying movement.
Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess (Cleveland et al., 1990): a robust, flexible decomposition that lets the seasonal pattern change slowly.
Variation caused by how many of each weekday a month contains; a month with five Saturdays sells more in a shop that is busy on Saturdays.
The slow-moving long-run level of a series.
The seasonal adjustment software used by the US Census Bureau and many statistics offices, combining moving-average filters, ARIMA extension of the series and calendar adjustments.
drill:
Work it out

Monthly sales. Two years ago the level was ~1,000 units/month and December ran ~200 above trend. This year the level is ~3,000 and December ran ~600 above trend. Next year's trend forecast for December is 3,500.

(a) Additive or multiplicative? (b) Forecast December under each assumption. (c) What single transform lets you use additive models anyway?

Answer

(a) Multiplicative. The swing scaled with the level: 200/1,000 = 600/3,000 = 20%. An additive seasonal component would have stayed near a constant number of units.

(b) Multiplicative: 3,500 × 1.20 = 4,200. Additive, using an average swing of ~400 units estimated over the two years: 3,500 + 400 = 3,900 — under-forecasting the peak month by 300 units, exactly the month where stock-outs are most expensive.

(c) Log. log(T × S) = log T + log S, so a 20% uplift becomes a constant +0.182 in log space. Fit additively on the log scale, then exponentiate — and apply a bias adjustment if you need the mean rather than the median.
qa: E
What are the components of a time series decomposition?

Trend: the slow-moving level. Seasonal: a pattern that repeats with a fixed, known period. Remainder: everything else. Some texts separate a cycle (rises and falls without a fixed period) from the trend; most methods fold it into a trend-cycle component.
E
How do you tell additive from multiplicative seasonality?

Plot the series and look at the seasonal swing as the level changes. A constant-size swing is additive; a swing that grows in proportion to the level is multiplicative. Numerically, check whether the peak's excess over trend is a constant number of units or a constant percentage. If multiplicative, log the series and treat it as additive.
Follow-up: What do you lose by modelling in logs? — The exponentiated forecast is the median, not the mean, so if you need the mean (for summing across products) you apply a bias adjustment.
E
Why does a 2×12 moving average appear for monthly data?

With an even period a 12-month average centred on a point is impossible: the window sits between two months. Averaging two consecutive 12-month averages centres it, which is the same as a 13-term weighted average with weights 1/24 at the ends and 1/12 in between. Every month gets equal weight, so the yearly seasonal pattern cancels out.
M
Walk me through classical additive decomposition.

Estimate the trend with a centred moving average of one seasonal period (2×m if m is even). Subtract it to get detrended values. Average the detrended values for each season (all Q1s, all Q2s). Centre those averages so they sum to zero; that is the seasonal component. Remainder = data − trend − seasonal.
Follow-up: What are its weaknesses? — No trend at the first and last m/2 points, a seasonal pattern frozen for all time, and outliers leaking into both trend and season.
M
Why is STL preferred over classical decomposition?

STL uses loess smoothing, so it lets the seasonal pattern evolve, produces estimates right up to the ends of the series, handles any period, and has a robust mode that down-weights outliers so one bad month does not bend the trend. Its two main knobs — the seasonal and trend window widths — let you choose how fast each component may change.
Follow-up: What does it not handle? — Calendar effects such as moving holidays and trading days, and multiplicative structure unless you log first.
M
Why can a fixed yearly seasonal term not model Easter or Diwali?

Because their dates move. Easter falls between 22 March and 25 April, so a pattern keyed to day-of-year spreads its effect over a month of wrong days. Use a holiday indicator (and a few days around it) as a regressor, as Prophet's holiday component does, or as X-13 does with its moving-holiday regressors.
M
How would you handle hourly electricity data with daily, weekly and yearly cycles?

Either MSTL, which extracts the 24-hour and 168-hour components in turn, or a regression with Fourier terms for each period — a few pairs for the daily and weekly cycles and more for the yearly shape — plus holiday indicators. Fourier terms handle a non-integer period like 365.25 days, which seasonal differencing cannot.
Follow-up: How do you choose the number of Fourier pairs? — Treat it as a hyperparameter and pick by backtest or an information criterion; too few smooths away real shape, too many fits noise.
M
What is a seasonally adjusted series and when is it misleading?

The series with its seasonal component removed, so month-to-month changes reflect underlying movement. It misleads at the end of the series, where the seasonal factors are least certain and get revised later, and around unusual periods — a pandemic year can distort the estimated seasonal factors for years after unless treated as an outlier.
M
How do you measure how seasonal a series is?

Seasonal strength F_S = max(0, 1 − Var(R) / Var(S + R)), with R the remainder and S the seasonal component from a decomposition. Near 0 means the seasonal pattern is lost in noise; near 1 means it dominates. Trend strength uses the trend in place of S. These features are useful for picking models across thousands of series.
H
Explain Prophet's model and its strengths and weaknesses.

Prophet writes y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε: a piecewise-linear or logistic trend with many candidate changepoints under a sparse Laplace prior, Fourier seasonality (by default 10 pairs yearly and 3 weekly), and holiday indicators, all fitted as a regression. Strengths: handles missing data and irregular timestamps, several seasonalities, moving holidays, and gives analysts interpretable knobs. Weaknesses: the residual has no autocorrelation structure, so short-term dynamics are ignored, and its trend extrapolation can be naive; on many benchmarks simple methods match or beat it.
Follow-up: When would you still use it? — For daily business series with strong calendar effects, many holidays and analysts who need to adjust forecasts by hand, as a solid baseline.
H
Your decomposition's remainder still shows a clear weekly pattern. What went wrong?

Either the period was set wrong (monthly instead of weekly), there are several seasonalities and only one was removed, the seasonal window was so wide that an evolving pattern was frozen, or there are calendar effects (trading days, holidays) leaking into the remainder. Check the remainder's autocorrelation at lags 7, 14, 21, try MSTL or more Fourier terms, and add calendar regressors.
H
Should you deseasonalise before training a gradient-boosted model?

Often not necessary: trees learn seasonality from calendar features (day of week, month) and lag-7 or lag-364 values, and a global model can learn it across series. Deseasonalising helps when series are short, when seasonality is multiplicative but the model is additive on raw units, or for models that extrapolate poorly. It adds a step that must be repeated identically at serving time; backtest both.
H
How did the pandemic affect seasonal adjustment, and what would you do in your own pipeline?

Huge, abrupt movements in 2020 entered the moving averages and seasonal estimates, so methods that treat everything as trend plus season would distort seasonal factors for the following years. The standard fix is to treat such periods as outliers or level shifts — explicit regressors that absorb them — so the seasonal estimate is based on normal years. In your own pipeline: flag the period, exclude or down-weight it when estimating seasonality, and check that the following years' seasonal factors look like pre-break years.

sum: What stationary means and why models need it; white noise and random walks; the ACF and PACF computed by hand on six values; differencing away trends and seasons; unit-root tests (ADF and KPSS); and the spurious-regression trap Granger and Newbold showed in 1974.

why:
In the 1920s the statistician George Udny Yule noticed something unsettling: across a run of years, the proportion of Church of England marriages and the mortality rate in England and Wales moved together so closely that their correlation was about 0.95. Nobody believed marriages in church were killing people. Both series had simply drifted downward over the same decades, and any two series that drift together look correlated, whatever they measure. Yule called these "nonsense correlations". Fifty years later Clive Granger and Paul Newbold showed by simulation that the problem is not a curiosity but the default outcome: regress one random wandering series on another, completely independent one, and the standard statistics declare a significant relationship most of the time.

The same trap catches engineers today. A dashboard shows that GPU spend and the number of support tickets have risen together all year with a correlation of 0.9; someone proposes that inference latency is driving complaints. A model trained to predict sales from web traffic fits beautifully in-sample, because both grew with the company, and falls apart when the two stop growing in step. A gradient-boosted model trained on a series that has doubled predicts a flat line at the training maximum, because trees cannot extrapolate.

All three failures come from one property, or rather its absence: stationarity. A stationary series behaves the same way statistically wherever you look at it: same average level, same spread, same relationship between today and yesterday. Most forecasting models, and all the standard statistics about correlation and significance, quietly assume it. When the assumption fails, averages computed from the past describe nothing stable, correlations measure shared drift, and significance tests lie.

This lesson makes the idea precise and gives you the tools to diagnose and fix it. You will meet white noise and the random walk, the two reference series of the whole field; compute autocorrelation by hand on six numbers; learn to read the autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plots that guide model choice in ts4; remove trends and seasons by differencing; test for unit roots with ADF and KPSS; and see the spurious-regression result reproduced in the lab, along with its cure.
primer:
A river and a drunkard

Two pictures carry most of the intuition. The first is the water level of a river at a fixed spot, measured daily over many years. It rises after rain and falls in dry spells, but it always comes back toward a typical level, and a wet week in 1990 looked statistically much like a wet week in 2020. Its average, its spread and the way today's level relates to yesterday's are the same in every decade. That is a stationary series: shocks happen, but they fade, and the series reverts to its mean.

The second picture is the classic "drunkard's walk": a person who takes one random step left or right each second. There is no typical position to come back to. After a hundred steps they are typically about ten steps from the start, after ten thousand steps about a hundred, and every step's effect is permanent. That is a random walk, and it is non-stationary: its spread grows with time and its "average level" is meaningless. Stock prices, exchange rates, many economic aggregates and many business metrics behave more like the drunkard than the river over the time scales we care about.

The analogy breaks in one place worth noticing. Plenty of business series are neither pure picture: a growing company's revenue is a drunkard walking up a slope (a random walk with drift), and a store's daily sales are a river whose level jumps when a competitor opens. Much of this lesson is about telling these cases apart and turning each into something stationary.

Why models want stationarity

A model learns from the past and applies what it learned to the future. That only works if the past and the future share the same rules. For a stationary series, an average or a correlation estimated over the last three years is an estimate of something fixed, and it will still hold next month. For a non-stationary series, the "average level of the last three years" is a number that will never be seen again. So the standard workflow is: transform the series until it is (close to) stationary, model the stationary version, then undo the transformation to forecast the original.

The two main tools

The first tool is the autocorrelation function (ACF): for each lag k, the correlation between the series and itself shifted k steps. It is the fingerprint of a series' memory. A stationary series' ACF drops toward zero within a few lags; a random walk's ACF stays near 1 for dozens of lags; a seasonal series shows spikes at the seasonal lag.

The second tool is differencing: replace each value with its change from the previous one. Differencing the drunkard's positions gives back the individual steps, which are independent random noise — perfectly stationary. Differencing a company's revenue gives its growth per period, which is far more stable than its level. When there is a seasonal pattern, a seasonal difference (this December minus last December) removes it.

A reader who stops here should hold this rule: before modelling or correlating, check whether the series is stationary; if not, transform it (log for growing swings, difference for trends and wandering, seasonal difference for stable seasons) until it is.
body:
1. Stationarity, defined

A series is strictly stationary if the joint distribution of any stretch of values is unchanged when you shift the stretch in time: (y_1, …, y_10) has the same distribution as (y_101, …, y_110). That is a strong requirement and impossible to check from data, so in practice we use weak stationarity (also called covariance stationarity), which asks only three things:

  • the mean E[y_t] is the same constant μ for every t;
  • the variance Var(y_t) is the same constant σ² for every t;
  • the covariance between y_t and y_{t−k} depends only on the lag k, not on t.

The third condition is the interesting one. It says the relationship between "today and yesterday" is the same in January and July, this year and ten years ago. That covariance, as a function of k, is the autocovariance γ(k); dividing by the variance γ(0) gives the autocorrelation ρ(k) = γ(k)/γ(0), which lies between −1 and 1 (the same normalisation that turns covariance into correlation in math3).

What breaks stationarity? A trend breaks the constant mean. A seasonal pattern also breaks it (the mean in December differs from the mean in June). A swing that grows with the level breaks constant variance. A structural break breaks everything. A random walk keeps a constant mean of zero increments but its variance grows with t, so it breaks the second condition.

One more property lurks in the background: ergodicity, the guarantee that averaging over time along one long series converges to the true average of the process. We usually have exactly one history — one record of this store's sales — so we can only learn the process's properties by averaging over time. Stationarity plus ergodicity is what makes that legitimate.

2. The two reference series: white noise and the random walk

White noise is a sequence ε_1, ε_2, … of values with mean zero, constant variance σ² and zero correlation between any two different time points. It is the formal version of "pure unpredictable noise". Its ACF is 1 at lag 0 and 0 at every other lag. Every model in this track can be described as a recipe that turns white noise into a structured series, and every model is judged by whether its residuals look like white noise: if they do, the model has extracted all the predictable structure.

A random walk accumulates white noise: y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t, starting from some y_0. Unrolling the recursion, y_t = y_0 + ε_1 + ε_2 + … + ε_t, a sum of t independent shocks, so Var(y_t) = tσ²: the spread grows linearly with time and the standard deviation as √t. Every shock stays in the series forever. A random walk with drift adds a constant: y_t = c + y_{t−1} + ε_t, so the series moves on average c per step, plus the wandering. The best forecast of a random walk is the last value (the naive forecast of ts1), and with drift it is the last value plus c·h.

3. The AR(1) process: the bridge between them

Between white noise and the random walk sits the autoregressive process of order 1, AR(1): y_t = φ·y_{t−1} + ε_t (add a constant to give it a non-zero mean). The coefficient φ controls memory. With φ = 0 it is white noise. With φ = 1 it is a random walk. For |φ| < 1 it is stationary: a shock's effect after k steps is φ^k, which fades. With φ = 0.8, a shock keeps 80% of its effect after one step, 64% after two, 33% after five and 11% after ten.

The same arithmetic gives the ACF. Substituting the equation into itself, y_t = φ^k·y_{t−k} + (shocks between t−k+1 and t). The shocks in between are independent of y_{t−k}, so the correlation between y_t and y_{t−k} is ρ(k) = φ^k: geometric decay. The lab simulates 400 points with φ = 0.8 and measures sample autocorrelations of 0.79, 0.64, 0.36 and 0.12 at lags 1, 2, 5 and 10, against theoretical values of 0.80, 0.64, 0.33 and 0.11. The value φ = 1 is the boundary where the decay stops; this is why a random walk is said to have a unit root — the coefficient on the lag equals one.

4. The sample ACF, computed by hand

Given data y_1 … y_n with mean ȳ, the sample autocorrelation at lag k is

r_k = Σ_{t=k+1..n} (y_t − ȳ)(y_{t−k} − ȳ)  /  Σ_{t=1..n} (y_t − ȳ)²

The numerator adds up products of deviations for every pair of points k apart; the denominator is the total sum of squared deviations. Take six values: 3, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7.

The mean is 33 / 6 = 5.5 and the sum of squared deviations is 17.5. For lag 1, multiply each deviation by the one before it: (−0.5)(−2.5) = 1.25, (−1.5)(−0.5) = 0.75, (0.5)(−1.5) = −0.75, (2.5)(0.5) = 1.25, (1.5)(2.5) = 3.75. These sum to 6.25, so r_1 = 6.25 / 17.5 ≈ 0.357. For lag 2, pair values two apart: (−1.5)(−2.5) = 3.75, (0.5)(−0.5) = −0.25, (2.5)(−1.5) = −3.75, (1.5)(0.5) = 0.75, summing to 0.5, so r_2 = 0.5 / 17.5 ≈ 0.029.

Two design choices in the formula deserve a word. It uses the overall mean, not separate means for the early and late values in each pair, and it divides by the full sum of squares rather than the sum over the n − k overlapping pairs. Both choices slightly shrink r_k toward zero at large lags (where few pairs exist, so estimates are noisy) and guarantee the set of autocorrelations is internally consistent, which matters when models are fitted from them.

How big must r_k be to matter? If the series were white noise, each sample autocorrelation would be roughly normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 1/√n, so about 95% would fall inside ±2/√n (more precisely ±1.96/√n). For n = 6, that band is ±0.82, so r_1 = 0.36 is entirely consistent with noise: six points can barely establish anything. For n = 400 the band is ±0.10, and a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.36 would be overwhelming evidence. Because you look at 20 or 40 lags at once, expect about one bar in twenty outside the band even for pure noise; a single marginal bar at an odd lag is rarely meaningful. To test a group of lags jointly, the Ljung-Box test combines the squared autocorrelations of lags 1 to h into one statistic, compared with a chi-squared distribution; it is the standard check that a model's residuals are white noise.

5. Reading an ACF

The ACF's shape tells you what kind of series you have. A slow, almost linear decay from near 1 is the signature of a trend or a unit root: values far apart are still similar because the series has wandered or trended. A geometric decay suggests a stationary autoregressive process. Spikes at the seasonal lag and its multiples (7, 14, 21 for daily data; 12, 24 for monthly; 24, 48 for hourly) show seasonality. A sharp cut-off after a few lags — significant at lags 1 and 2, then nothing — suggests a moving-average process, introduced next. An ACF that is all inside the band means there is little linear structure left, as you want for residuals.

A practical warning: do not read model orders from the ACF of a series that is not stationary. Its ACF is dominated by the slow decay and hides everything else. Difference first, then read.

6. The PACF and the MA process

The ACF at lag 2 mixes two things: the direct relationship between y_t and y_{t−2}, and the indirect one passing through y_{t−1}. In an AR(1), y_{t−2} affects y_t only through y_{t−1}, yet r_2 = φ² is non-zero. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) removes the indirect path: the partial autocorrelation at lag k is the coefficient on y_{t−k} in a regression of y_t on y_{t−1}, …, y_{t−k}. For an AR(1), the PACF is φ at lag 1 and zero afterwards, because once y_{t−1} is in the regression, y_{t−2} adds nothing. For an AR(p), the PACF cuts off after lag p.

The mirror image is the moving-average process, MA(q), where the value is a weighted sum of the current and q previous shocks: an MA(1) is y_t = ε_t + θ·ε_{t−1}. Values more than q steps apart share no shocks, so the ACF cuts off after lag q (an MA(1) has ρ(1) = θ/(1 + θ²) and zero beyond), while the PACF decays gradually. This pair of rules — AR: ACF decays, PACF cuts off; MA: ACF cuts off, PACF decays — is the classic Box-Jenkins identification method that ts4 uses to choose ARIMA orders.

7. Differencing

The first difference is Δy_t = y_t − y_{t−1}, the change from one step to the next. Differencing the six values above gives 5 − 3 = 2, 4 − 5 = −1, 6 − 4 = 2, 8 − 6 = 2 and 7 − 8 = −1. The original values rose from 3 to 7; the differences hover around their mean of 0.8 with no trend. That mean is the drift: the average change per step. A forecast of the differences (say 0.8 per step) is turned back into a forecast of the level by adding it up from the last value: 7.8, 8.6, 9.4 for the next three steps. This is exactly the drift method of ts4.

Why does differencing work? For a random walk, Δy_t = ε_t, white noise: the difference undoes the accumulation. For a linear trend y_t = a + bt + noise, Δy_t = b + (noise_t − noise_{t−1}): the trend becomes a constant. For a quadratic trend, one difference leaves a linear trend and a second difference (the difference of the differences) is needed; in practice a second difference is rarely required and two is the maximum anyone uses.

Seasonal differencing subtracts the value one season earlier: y_t − y_{t−m}. If December is always 200 units above the yearly level, December minus last December cancels those 200 units, along with the seasonal effect of every other month. It also removes a trend partially (a December-to-December difference contains a year of growth, now a constant), so sometimes a seasonal difference alone makes a series stationary. When both are needed, you apply both: (y_t − y_{t−m}) − (y_{t−1} − y_{t−m−1}). The order does not matter.

Differencing has a cost. Each difference loses one observation at the start (a seasonal difference loses m), and differencing amplifies short-term noise. Most importantly, over-differencing — differencing a series that was already stationary — creates structure that was not there. Differencing white noise gives ε_t − ε_{t−1}, which has twice the variance and a lag-1 autocorrelation of exactly −0.5. So a strongly negative lag-1 ACF after differencing, or a variance that went up rather than down, says you differenced once too often.

8. Deterministic versus stochastic trends

Two different processes can both look like "a rising line with noise". A trend-stationary series is a straight line plus stationary noise: y_t = a + bt + u_t with u_t stationary. If a shock pushes it above the line, it drifts back. A difference-stationary series is a random walk with drift: shocks are permanent, and after a shock the series continues from the new level. The two need different treatments: for a trend-stationary series you subtract the fitted line (detrend); for a difference-stationary series you difference. They also give very different forecasts far ahead. Trend-stationary forecast intervals stay a constant width around the line; random-walk intervals widen like √h forever. Deciding which you have is what unit-root tests are for.

9. Unit-root tests: ADF and KPSS

The Dickey-Fuller test starts from the AR(1) equation and subtracts y_{t−1} from both sides: Δy_t = c + γ·y_{t−1} + ε_t, where γ = φ − 1. A unit root (φ = 1) means γ = 0; a stationary series has γ < 0 (the further above its mean the series sits, the more it tends to fall back). So the test regresses the differences on the lagged level and looks at the t-statistic of γ. The twist is that under the null hypothesis of a unit root, this t-statistic does not follow the usual distribution, so the usual ±1.96 cut-off is wrong. With a constant in the regression, the 5% critical value is about −2.87 for a few hundred observations: you need a t-statistic below −2.87, not −1.96, to reject a unit root. The augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test adds a few lagged differences Δy_{t−1}, Δy_{t−2}, … to the regression so that short-term correlation in the errors does not distort the result. In the lab, the AR(1) series with φ = 0.8 gives a t-statistic of −6.82 (unit root rejected) and the random walk −1.21 (not rejected).

ADF has a known weakness: low power. A stationary series with φ = 0.95 looks so much like a random walk over a few hundred points that the test often fails to reject. Failing to reject is not evidence of a unit root; it may just be too little data. The KPSS test flips the hypotheses: its null is that the series is stationary (around a level, or around a linear trend), and it rejects when the cumulative sums of deviations from the mean wander too far. Using the two together gives four outcomes. ADF rejects and KPSS does not: stationary. ADF does not reject and KPSS rejects: unit root, so difference. Both reject: often a structural break or a series with very long memory. Neither rejects: the data cannot decide, so lean on the plot, the domain and backtests. Automated tools such as auto.arima in R's forecast package use repeated KPSS tests to choose the number of differences.

10. Spurious regression

Regression of one series on another assumes the residuals are stationary. Granger and Newbold's 1974 simulation made the failure vivid. Generate two completely independent random walks of 50 observations, regress one on the other, and test whether the slope is zero at the 5% level. If the standard theory applied, you would wrongly find a "significant" relationship 5% of the time. They found one 76% of the time. Later simulations by Granger and colleagues show the rate climbing with the sample size — 77% at 100 observations and 97.6% at 10,000 — because more data does not help when the assumption is broken; it only makes the false precision worse. Even two independent but highly persistent stationary series (AR(1) with φ = 0.9) gave false rejections about 52% of the time at every sample size, so the problem is not confined to unit roots: strong autocorrelation inflates t-statistics whenever the standard errors ignore it.

The lab repeats the experiment: across 1,000 pairs of independent 50-step random walks, |t| exceeded 1.96 in 66% of regressions (the original paper's 76% came from 100 replications, so some variation is expected); regressing the differences of the walks instead gave 5.7%, close to the correct 5%. The practical rule follows directly: never regress levels on levels for wandering series unless you have a reason to believe they are cointegrated (next section, and deep); regress changes on changes, or include lagged values of the target so the residuals are stationary, and check the residual ACF.

11. Variance stabilisation comes first

Stationarity also requires constant variance. If the seasonal swing or the noise grows with the level, difference the log, not the raw series: the first difference of the log is approximately the percentage change, Δlog y_t ≈ (y_t − y_{t−1}) / y_{t−1}, which is usually far more stable than the change in units. Revenue growing from 1 million to 10 million a month with 5% monthly noise has unit changes that grow tenfold but log-differences with a steady spread. The order is always: transform for variance (log or Box-Cox, ts2), then difference for mean, then read the ACF.
deep:
Cointegration: when levels regressions are legitimate

Some non-stationary series genuinely move together because something ties them. The price of a stock and the price of its futures contract both wander like random walks, but arbitrage keeps the gap between them small and mean-reverting. Two such series are cointegrated: each has a unit root, but a linear combination (price minus futures price, or y − βx in general) is stationary. In that case regressing the levels is meaningful — it estimates the long-run relationship — and differencing both would throw that relationship away. The Engle-Granger method tests for cointegration by regressing y on x in levels and running a unit-root test on the residuals (with adjusted critical values); if the residuals are stationary, the series are cointegrated. An error-correction model then combines short-run changes with a term that pulls the series back toward the long-run relationship. For engineers, the takeaway is that "difference everything" is a safe default for correlation questions but loses information when there is a real equilibrium, such as supply and demand at different points of the same pipeline.

Why the Dickey-Fuller distribution is non-standard

Under the unit-root null, y_{t−1} is itself a random walk, so its variance grows over time and the usual central-limit arguments for the slope estimate do not apply. The estimate of γ converges to zero faster than usual (at rate 1/n instead of 1/√n) and its t-statistic follows a skewed distribution, now called the Dickey-Fuller distribution, tabulated by simulation. Its critical values depend on whether the regression includes a constant, or a constant and a linear trend: about −1.95 with neither, −2.86 with a constant, and −3.41 with a constant and trend, at the 5% level for large samples (slightly more negative for small ones). Choosing the wrong version is a common error: testing a trending series without a trend term can make a trend-stationary series look like a unit root.

Structural breaks fool unit-root tests

A stationary series with a single permanent level shift looks, to a unit-root test, like a series whose shocks are permanent — because one shock was. Perron showed in 1989 that ignoring a break biases the ADF test toward not rejecting a unit root. The practical consequences: before testing, plot the series and look for breaks (a product launch, a pricing change, a pandemic); include a break dummy in the test regression if you know the date; and consider whether a model with a level-shift regressor describes the series better than differencing. Change-point detection (ts10) finds breaks you do not know about.

Long memory and fractional differencing

Some series sit between stationary and unit-root: their ACF decays, but far more slowly than geometrically, following a power law. River flows (the Nile, studied by Hurst), network traffic and volatility in financial returns behave this way. The model for this is the fractionally integrated process, which differences by a non-integer amount d between 0 and 0.5: the operator (1 − L)^d, where L shifts the series back one step, is expanded into an infinite weighted sum of past values with slowly decaying weights. Fractional differencing removes just enough memory to make the series stationary while keeping more of the long-run information than a full difference would. It is used in quantitative finance feature engineering to make price series stationary without destroying their predictive memory. Both ADF and KPSS rejecting is a hint that long memory may be present.

Effective sample size and comparing forecasters

Autocorrelation shrinks the information content of a sample. For an AR(1) with coefficient φ, the variance of the sample mean is approximately σ²/n × (1 + φ)/(1 − φ), so the effective sample size is n(1 − φ)/(1 + φ). With φ = 0.8 that is n/9: 900 hourly observations behave like about 100 independent ones. The same logic applies to forecast errors: errors from consecutive origins in a backtest are correlated, so a difference in average error between two models can look significant on a naive t-test and not be. The Diebold-Mariano test (ts5) compares two forecasters' errors with a standard error that accounts for this autocorrelation.

Stationarity for ML forecasters

Modern forecasters handle non-stationarity in their own ways, and recognising them as stationarity tricks helps in interviews. Gradient-boosted trees predict a piecewise-constant function of their inputs, so they cannot produce a value larger than any target seen in training; on a growing series they flatten out. The fixes are to predict the difference from the last value, the ratio to a recent mean, or the log ratio — all targets that stay in a stable range. DeepAR scales each series by its average, PatchTST and many others apply per-window normalisation (subtract the window mean, divide by its standard deviation, add them back after prediction, sometimes called RevIN), and foundation models like Chronos scale each context by its mean absolute value (ts7, ts9). Each converts a non-stationary level problem into a closer-to-stationary shape problem.

Seasonal unit roots and the choice between differencing and Fourier terms

A seasonal pattern can itself wander: the December peak may drift up and down from year to year without returning to a fixed size. That is a seasonal unit root, removed by seasonal differencing. If instead the seasonal pattern is stable, seasonal differencing over-differences at the seasonal lag (the ACF shows a strong negative spike at lag m), and a deterministic seasonal model — dummies or Fourier terms (ts2) — is better. Tests exist for seasonal unit roots (the OCSB and Canova-Hansen tests are used by automatic ARIMA tools), but the practical check is the same as for ordinary differencing: if the ACF at lag m goes strongly negative after seasonal differencing, you probably did not need it.
prod:
Where these ideas bite in real systems

Correlation dashboards. Observability tools make it easy to overlay two metrics and compute their correlation. For trending or wandering metrics this almost always produces high correlations that mean nothing; incident reviews that blame a metric because it "correlated 0.9 with the outage metric over the past month" are reasoning about shared drift. Correlate changes (first differences, or residuals after removing seasonality), not levels, and require a mechanism.

Trees on growing targets. A capacity model built with gradient-boosted trees on raw request counts flattens out at the training-set maximum; on a fast-growing product the forecast falls further and further below reality each week. Symptoms: residuals that grow in one direction over time and forecasts that never exceed a ceiling. The fix is to predict a ratio to a recent level or a log difference.

Drift that changes the rules. Production monitoring of model inputs often uses statistical distance between the training distribution and the live distribution. For non-stationary features (anything that grows, such as counts of users), that distance grows every day by construction and the alert becomes noise. Monitor stationary transformations — growth rates, ratios, per-user rates — instead.

A/B tests on time-series metrics. Daily active users or revenue per day are autocorrelated, so standard errors that treat each day as independent are too small, and a two-week test looks more precise than it is. Analysts use per-user metrics where possible, or methods that account for autocorrelation, and pre-period adjustments that remove persistent differences.

The case: Granger and Newbold, and what came after

Granger and Newbold's 1974 paper in the Journal of Econometrics was aimed at applied economists who reported regressions between trending macroeconomic series with high R² values and significant t-statistics, but with residuals that were strongly autocorrelated (a low Durbin-Watson statistic). Their simulation of independent random walks showed that such results should be expected even when there is no relationship at all: about three-quarters of regressions at their sample size of 50 produced a "significant" slope. Phillips later supplied the theory (1986): with unit roots, the t-statistic does not converge to a normal distribution but grows with the sample size, so rejection rates approach 100%. A 1998 follow-up by Granger, Hyung and Jeon quantified it: 77% false rejections at 100 observations and 97.6% at 10,000 for random walks, and around 52% for independent stationary series with φ = 0.9 regardless of sample size. The work changed econometric practice — unit-root testing, differencing and cointegration became standard — and Granger shared the 2003 Nobel prize in economics for the cointegration work that grew out of it. For an AI engineer, its lesson is general: standard errors assume independence, and time-series data violates it, so impressive statistics on raw levels are a warning sign, not evidence.

Practical checklist and tooling

In Python, statsmodels provides the ACF and PACF (with plotting helpers), the ADF test (adfuller), KPSS (kpss), the Ljung-Box test (acorr_ljungbox) and an ndiffs-style workflow through its ARIMA tools; the pmdarima and statsforecast libraries automate "how many differences?" with repeated KPSS tests. The checklist an experienced forecaster runs on a new series: plot it; log if the swing grows with the level; look at the ACF for slow decay and seasonal spikes; run ADF and KPSS with the right deterministic terms; difference the minimum needed; re-plot the ACF; check the differenced series' variance went down; and after modelling, check that residuals pass a Ljung-Box test.

Knobs

The knobs are the transform, the number of ordinary and seasonal differences, the deterministic terms in the unit-root test (none, constant, constant and trend), the number of augmenting lags in ADF (chosen by an information criterion), the number of lags in the Ljung-Box test (often 10 for non-seasonal data and 2m for seasonal), and the treatment of known breaks. Every one of them should be written down with the model, because changing any of them changes forecasts.
myths: Stationary means the series is flat.

Stationary means the statistical behaviour does not change over time: the same mean, the same spread and the same pattern of correlation between values k steps apart, wherever you look. A stationary series can wiggle a lot — white noise wiggles constantly — as long as the wiggling looks the same in every stretch.
A high correlation between two series means they are related.

Not if both are trending or wandering. Granger and Newbold showed in 1974 that regressing one random walk on an independent one gives a 'significant' slope about three times out of four at 50 observations, and later work found the rate approaches 100% as the sample grows. Difference both series, or test for cointegration, before believing it.
Differencing is always safe, so difference when in doubt.

Differencing a series that was already stationary (over-differencing) adds a negative correlation at lag 1 and inflates forecast variance. The tell-tale sign is a lag-1 autocorrelation near −0.5 after differencing. Use a unit-root test and the ACF to decide, and difference the minimum number of times.
If the ADF test does not reject, the series has a unit root.

Failing to reject is not proof. ADF has low power: with a few hundred points it often cannot tell a unit root from a strongly persistent stationary series (φ = 0.95). That is why practitioners pair it with KPSS, whose null hypothesis is the opposite, and look at the ACF.
Machine-learning models do not care about stationarity.

Tree models cannot extrapolate beyond the target values they saw in training, so a trending target makes them predict a flat ceiling; neural networks trained on raw levels struggle when test values sit outside the training range. Modern ML forecasters handle this by differencing, by predicting ratios to a recent level, or by normalising each window — all ways of making the target closer to stationary.
lab:
Goal: compute the ACF by hand-written code, watch an AR(1) match φ^k, see a random walk's ACF refuse to decay and its differences become white noise, run a Dickey-Fuller regression, and reproduce Granger and Newbold's spurious regressions. NumPy only, gpt_env (Python 3.12). Save as ts3.py.

import numpy as np

def acf(x, nlags):
    """Sample autocorrelation, the textbook way: one mean, one denominator."""
    d = np.asarray(x, float) - np.mean(x)
    den = np.sum(d * d)
    return np.array([np.sum(d[k:] * d[:len(d) - k]) / den for k in range(nlags + 1)])

# 1. The worked example from the lesson
y6 = [3, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7]
print("ACF of the 6 values:", np.round(acf(y6, 2), 3), " band +-", round(2 / np.sqrt(6), 2))
print("first differences:", np.diff(y6))

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 400
e = rng.normal(size=n)
ar = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    ar[t] = 0.8 * ar[t - 1] + e[t]          # stationary AR(1), phi = 0.8
rw = np.cumsum(e)                           # random walk: phi = 1
band = 2 / np.sqrt(n)
print(f"\nband = +-{band:.3f}")
print("AR(1) phi=0.8  ACF lags 1,2,5,10:", np.round(acf(ar, 10)[[1, 2, 5, 10]], 2), " theory 0.8^k:", np.round(0.8 ** np.array([1, 2, 5, 10]), 2))
print("random walk    ACF lags 1,2,5,10:", np.round(acf(rw, 10)[[1, 2, 5, 10]], 2))
print("diff(rw)       ACF lags 1,2,5,10:", np.round(acf(np.diff(rw), 10)[[1, 2, 5, 10]], 2))

def ols_t(yv, xv):
    """t-statistic of the slope in y = a + b x + u, with the usual i.i.d. standard error."""
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(xv)), xv])
    w, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, yv, rcond=None)
    resid = yv - X @ w
    s2 = resid @ resid / (len(yv) - 2)
    se = np.sqrt(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[1, 1])
    return w[1] / se

# 2. Dickey-Fuller regression: diff(y)_t = a + gamma * y_{t-1}; unit root means gamma = 0.
#    5% critical value for the t-statistic (with constant, n about 250-500) is about -2.87, not -1.96.
for name, s in (("AR(1)", ar), ("random walk", rw)):
    print(f"DF t-stat {name:12s}: {ols_t(np.diff(s), s[:-1]):6.2f}  (reject unit root if below -2.87)")

# 3. Granger-Newbold: regress one independent random walk on another, 1,000 times
for label, make in (("levels", lambda: (np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=50)), np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=50)))),
                    ("differences", lambda: (rng.normal(size=49), rng.normal(size=49)))):
    hits = sum(abs(ols_t(*make())) > 1.96 for _ in range(1000))
    print(f"independent walks, {label:11s}: |t| > 1.96 in {hits / 10:.1f}% of regressions")

Run: python ts3.py. Output from a test run:

ACF of the 6 values: [1.    0.357 0.029]  band +- 0.82
first differences: [ 2 -1  2  2 -1]

band = +-0.100
AR(1) phi=0.8  ACF lags 1,2,5,10: [0.79 0.64 0.36 0.12]  theory 0.8^k: [0.8  0.64 0.33 0.11]
random walk    ACF lags 1,2,5,10: [0.99 0.97 0.93 0.86]
diff(rw)       ACF lags 1,2,5,10: [-0.04  0.01  0.03 -0.04]
DF t-stat AR(1)       :  -6.82  (reject unit root if below -2.87)
DF t-stat random walk :  -1.21  (reject unit root if below -2.87)
independent walks, levels     : |t| > 1.96 in 66.4% of regressions
independent walks, differences: |t| > 1.96 in 5.7% of regressions

What to look for. The first line reproduces the hand calculation. The AR(1) sample ACF tracks 0.8^k closely; the random walk's ACF is still 0.86 at lag 10 (a classic unit-root picture), and differencing it leaves every autocorrelation inside ±0.10. The Dickey-Fuller t-statistics fall on opposite sides of −2.87. The last two lines are the spurious-regression result: two-thirds of regressions between unrelated walks look significant in levels, about the nominal 5% in differences.

Try next. Set φ = 0.97 and re-run the Dickey-Fuller line a few times with different seeds: the test often fails to reject even though the series is stationary — low power. Increase the walk length from 50 to 1,000 and watch the levels rejection rate climb toward 100%.
recap: A series is (weakly) stationary when its mean, variance and autocorrelation at each lag do not change over time; most classical models assume it, because only then do statistics estimated from the past describe the future.
White noise has no autocorrelation at all; a random walk adds each new shock to the previous value, so its variance grows over time and it is not stationary.

The autocorrelation at lag k compares each value with the value k steps earlier, using the overall mean and variance; on the six values 3, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7 the lag-1 autocorrelation is 6.25 / 17.5 ≈ 0.36.
For white noise, about 95% of sample autocorrelations fall inside ±2/√n, so bars outside that band suggest real structure.
An AR(1) series with coefficient φ has autocorrelation φ^k at lag k, decaying geometrically; its partial autocorrelation has one spike at lag 1.
First differencing (y_t − y_{t−1}) removes a stochastic or linear trend; seasonal differencing (y_t − y_{t−m}) removes a stable seasonal pattern.
The ADF test's null is a unit root (non-stationary) and the KPSS test's null is stationarity, so using both gives a clearer verdict than either alone.
Regressing one non-stationary series on another can produce impressive but meaningless fits — spurious regression — unless the series are cointegrated.
Over-differencing shows up as a lag-1 autocorrelation near −0.5 and makes forecasts worse.
glossary: The list of autocorrelations at lags 1, 2, 3 and so on, usually drawn as a bar chart called a correlogram.
A test whose null hypothesis is that the series has a unit root; rejecting it is evidence of stationarity. 'Augmented' means extra lagged differences are added to soak up short-term correlation.
An autoregressive process of order 1: y_t = c + φ·y_{t−1} + ε_t. Stationary when |φ| < 1; a random walk when φ = 1.
AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average: the classical model family that differences a series d times and then models it with p autoregressive and q moving-average terms. Taught in ts4.
The correlation between a series and itself shifted by k steps (lag k).
The covariance between a series and itself shifted by k steps; dividing by the variance gives the autocorrelation.
When two non-stationary series share a common stochastic trend, so that some combination of them is stationary; regression between them is then meaningful.
A bar chart of the ACF (or PACF) against lag, with significance bands.
Replacing each value with its change from the previous value (first differencing) or from the value one season earlier (seasonal differencing).
A constant average change per step in a random walk; the mean of the first differences.
The property that averages over time from one long series converge to the true averages of the process; it is what lets us learn from a single history.
Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin test, whose null hypothesis is that the series is stationary (around a level or a trend); rejecting it is evidence of a unit root.
A shift back in time by k steps; y_{t−k} is the lag-k value of y_t.
A test of whether a group of autocorrelations (say lags 1 to 10) are jointly zero; used to check that model residuals are white noise.
A moving-average process of order q: each value is the current shock plus a weighted sum of the previous q shocks, so values more than q steps apart are uncorrelated.
Differencing a series that was already stationary; it creates spurious negative lag-1 autocorrelation and increases forecast variance.
The correlation between y_t and y_{t−k} after removing the effects of the lags in between; it shows the direct effect of each lag.
A series where each value is the previous value plus an independent shock: y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t. Its variance grows without limit.
Replacing y_t with y_t − y_{t−m}, where m is the seasonal period; removes a stable seasonal pattern.
A regression between unrelated non-stationary series that shows a large R² and a 'significant' slope purely because both series wander.
The whole joint distribution of any stretch of values is unchanged by shifting it in time. Stronger than weak stationarity and rarely testable.
Constant mean, constant variance and autocovariances that depend only on the lag, not on time.
A series that becomes stationary after subtracting a deterministic trend line; shocks to it fade away.
The property of a process like a random walk (φ = 1 in AR(1)) whose shocks never fade; the series is non-stationary and becomes stationary after differencing.
A series of uncorrelated values with mean zero and constant variance; the building block of all the models in this track.
drill:
Work it out

(a) An AR(1) process has φ = 0.8. What are its theoretical ACF values at lags 1, 2 and 5, and what does its PACF look like?

(b) You have n = 400 daily points. The ACF reads 0.98, 0.97, 0.95, 0.94 … still 0.80 at lag 30. ADF p = 0.61, KPSS p = 0.01. What is the significance band, what is going on, and what do you do?

Answer

(a) For AR(1), ρ(k) = φᵏ: lag 1 = 0.80, lag 2 = 0.64, lag 5 = 0.8⁵ ≈ 0.33 — geometric decay. The PACF has a single spike of 0.8 at lag 1 and is ~0 afterwards, because once lag 1 is accounted for, older lags add nothing.

(b) Band = ±1.96/√400 = ±0.098. An ACF that barely decays is the signature of a unit root or strong trend, and the tests agree: ADF cannot reject a unit root (its null), KPSS rejects stationarity (its null). First-difference, re-plot the ACF, re-run both tests, and check the differenced variance went down. If weekly spikes at 7 and 14 then appear, add a seasonal difference or weekly seasonal terms. Do not read AR/MA orders off the undifferenced ACF — they are meaningless there.
qa: E
What does it mean for a series to be stationary?

Its statistical properties do not depend on when you look: constant mean, constant variance, and an autocorrelation between values k apart that depends only on k. That is weak stationarity; strict stationarity requires the whole distribution to be time-invariant. Trends, growing variance and changing seasonal patterns all break it.
E
What is the autocorrelation function and how do you read it?

The ACF gives the correlation between the series and itself at lag 1, 2, 3 and so on, plotted as bars with a ±2/√n band. Bars outside the band suggest real correlation. Slow decay suggests a trend or unit root, spikes at the seasonal lag (7, 12, 24) suggest seasonality, and a sharp cut-off after lag q suggests a moving-average process.
E
What does first differencing do, and what is its seasonal version?

First differencing replaces y_t with y_t − y_{t−1}, the change per step; it removes a linear or stochastic trend. Seasonal differencing replaces y_t with y_t − y_{t−m}, the change from the same season last cycle; it removes a stable seasonal pattern. You forecast the differences and add them back up.
M
ADF and KPSS disagree. What does each test's null say, and how do you combine them?

ADF's null is a unit root; KPSS's null is stationarity. Both point the same way when ADF rejects and KPSS does not (stationary) or ADF does not reject and KPSS does (unit root, so difference). If both reject, the series may be stationary around a structural break or have long memory; if neither rejects, the data cannot tell — look at the ACF and the domain, and backtest models with and without differencing.
Follow-up: Why not rely on one test? — ADF has low power against persistent stationary series, so a non-rejection is weak evidence; pairing tests with opposite nulls reduces that risk.
M
Compute the lag-1 autocorrelation of 3, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7.

The mean is 5.5, so deviations are −2.5, −0.5, −1.5, 0.5, 2.5, 1.5 with sum of squares 17.5. Neighbouring products sum to 1.25 + 0.75 − 0.75 + 1.25 + 3.75 = 6.25. r_1 = 6.25 / 17.5 ≈ 0.36. With n = 6 the band is ±2/√6 ≈ ±0.82, so it is not significant — six points cannot establish much.

Follow-up: Why use the full-series denominator rather than the n−1 overlapping pairs? — It keeps the estimated autocorrelations a valid (positive-definite) set and shrinks noisy high-lag estimates toward zero.
M
Why is regressing one trending series on another dangerous?

Two independent series that both wander or trend will look correlated because they share 'going up over time', not because one drives the other. The usual standard errors assume stationary residuals, so t-statistics are wildly inflated. Granger and Newbold found 'significant' slopes in about 76% of regressions between independent random walks of length 50. Difference first, or test for cointegration.

Follow-up: What is cointegration? — Two non-stationary series sharing one stochastic trend, so a linear combination is stationary, like a stock's price and its futures price; then the levels relationship is real.
M
How do you tell an AR process from an MA process using the ACF and PACF?

An AR(p) process has an ACF that decays gradually and a PACF that cuts off after lag p. An MA(q) process has an ACF that cuts off after lag q and a PACF that decays. Mixed ARMA processes decay in both. This is the classic identification rule ts4 uses to choose ARIMA orders.
M
Why does an AR(1) series have autocorrelation φ^k?

Substitute repeatedly: y_t = φ y_{t−1} + ε_t = φ² y_{t−2} + φ ε_{t−1} + ε_t, and so on. The value k steps back enters with weight φ^k and the shocks in between are independent of it, so the correlation is φ^k. With φ = 0.8 that is 0.8, 0.64 and 0.33 at lags 1, 2 and 5.
M
How do you detect over-differencing?

After differencing, a lag-1 autocorrelation close to −0.5 and a larger variance than before are the signatures: differencing white noise gives ε_t − ε_{t−1}, whose lag-1 autocorrelation is exactly −0.5 and whose variance is doubled. Compare variances before and after; the right amount of differencing usually gives the smallest standard deviation.
H
What is a unit root, intuitively, and why does it matter for forecasting?

A unit root means shocks are permanent: in y_t = φ y_{t−1} + ε_t with φ = 1, today's shock stays in every future value. With φ < 1 shocks fade and the series reverts to its mean. For forecasting, a unit-root series has prediction intervals that widen without limit (like σ√h), while a stationary series' intervals level off. Mistaking one for the other gives overconfident or underconfident long-horizon intervals.

Follow-up: How would you distinguish trend-stationary from difference-stationary? — Fit both (linear trend with stationary errors vs differenced model), compare backtests and unit-root tests with a trend term; after a shock, trend-stationary series return to the line, difference-stationary ones do not.
H
Does a global ML forecaster need stationary inputs?

It needs a target whose distribution at test time resembles training. Trees cannot predict outside the range of targets they saw, so a growing series gets a flat ceiling. Common fixes: predict differences or ratios to the last value or a recent mean, normalise each input window by its own scale (as DeepAR and PatchTST do), and use lag features rather than raw levels. Each is a way of making the learning problem closer to stationary.
H
A metric's ACF shows tall bars at lags 24, 48, 72 that decay slowly, plus a slow overall decay. What is your modelling plan?

Slow overall decay means a trend or unit root; repeated spikes at multiples of 24 mean a daily seasonality in hourly data. Take logs if the swing grows with the level, apply a first difference and a seasonal difference at lag 24 (or model the daily cycle with Fourier terms), re-plot the ACF, and check for a weekly pattern at lag 168. Then choose orders from the remaining ACF and PACF, and verify the residuals are white noise with a Ljung-Box test.
H
Explain why the standard errors of an average are too small for autocorrelated data, with numbers.

The variance of a mean of n correlated values includes all the covariances between them. For an AR(1) with φ = 0.8 the effective sample size is about n(1 − φ)/(1 + φ) = n/9, so 900 hourly points carry the information of about 100 independent ones and the standard error is three times larger than σ/√n suggests. This matters when comparing two models on a backtest or reading an A/B test on a time-series metric.
